sections.title: How to use this toolkit
sections.html:
Read sections 1–5 in order. Section 1 establishes which records can be counted. Sections 2–3 summarize them. Section 4 chooses displays. Section 5 turns the evidence into a bounded decision. Recalculate each worked result before using a tool, then use the Excel 365 and SPSS routes to check it.

The course has no required textbook. The Albright and Winston, Field, and Knaflic headings in the crosswalk are scope cues, not claims that those chapters have been assigned or read. The core mapping is H001–H046, with some chart types treated briefly because this case does not call for them. H047–H058 are an optional design bridge. The original synthesis below is grounded in the open and primary sources actually cited; no textbook passage or page number is reproduced.

This source has no stable PDF pages. Use its stable numbered section headings, rather than page numbers, for future slide and PNP cross-references after pagination. S02 introduced grain and KPI framing. Sampling uncertainty begins in S05; tests and A/B decisions begin in S06. Neither is needed to describe these records.

sections.title: Running case: Cedar Lane Repair’s pickup desk
sections.html:
Cedar Lane Repair is fictional. Its manager must decide whether to extend pickup-desk staffing next week. The proposed KPI is the percentage of completed pickups served within 10 minutes of customer arrival. The provisional target is at least 90%; a data-quality guardrail requires no more than 5% missing waits. These are fictional managerial thresholds, not statistical standards.

The intended population for that decision is all pickup visits at this desk next week. The available evidence is narrower: one convenience extract from September 7–11, 2026. Its grain is one pickup visit per visit ID, not one customer or one day. Wait is a numeric variable in minutes; arrival day and pickup channel are categorical variables.

Visit IDDayChannelRecorded wait, minutes
101MonWalk-in4
102MonScheduled5
103TueWalk-in6
104TueScheduled7
105WedWalk-in8
106WedScheduled9
107ThuWalk-in10
108ThuScheduled31
109FriWalk-inMissing

Source and limits. A desk export supplies visit IDs and arrival days; a service log supplies waits. Both are fictional. The raw join produced 10 rows because visit 104 appeared twice in the export. The table above shows the 9 distinct visits after that duplicate was checked. Wait 31 is recorded but not yet verified against timestamps; visit 109 has no wait. The extract has few visits, uneven daily coverage, and no evidence that next week will resemble this week. Customer names are unnecessary for this analysis.

sections.title: 1. Establish trustworthy records
1.1 Grain, provenance, and duplicate checks
sections.html:
Grain states what one row represents: here, one visit ID represents one pickup visit. Provenance records where a value came from: here, the desk export identifies visits, while the service log supplies minutes. Check both before counting. A visit-level table is appropriate for a visit-level service KPI; counting export rows instead would give extra weight to visit 104. Penn State’s distinction between cases, variables, and populations helps keep those units separate (Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a).

Worked check. Start with 10 raw rows. List their visit IDs and count how often each appears. ID 104 has two raw appearances; every other ID has one. Compare the two 104 records with the source logs. Under this case’s stated finding—that they are repeat exports of the same visit—retain one. The result is 10 raw rows − 1 repeat = 9 distinct visits. If the records instead represented separate visits sharing an erroneous ID, investigate the key; do not silently delete either.

Excel 365 route. Put raw IDs in column A, beginning at A2. In a new column, enter =COUNTIF($A$2:A2,A2) and fill down. The first 104 returns 1 and its second appearance returns 2. Filter values above 1 for source review; do not treat the formula alone as permission to remove a row. After reconciliation, make the nine-row range an Excel Table named Visits. Table headers support filtering and sorting, while structured references such as Visits[WaitMin] make the summarized column explicit (Microsoft, n.d.-a; Microsoft, n.d.-b).

SPSS route. Import the reconciled, nine-visit file, with VisitID as an identifier, Channel and Day as categorical variables, and WaitMin as a scale variable. Compare the imported case count (9) and each ID against the reconciled list before producing statistics. Keep the raw export separately so the reconciliation can be inspected.

Failure mode: “Ten rows means ten visits.” It does not when a source can repeat a key.

Try it — ungraded. Suppose ID 105 is also exported twice, and source review confirms another exact repeat. How many distinct visits should remain from the now 11 raw rows? Explained answer: 9. There are two repeat rows above the nine distinct visits: 11−2=911-2=9. The source check, not the arithmetic alone, establishes that they are repeats.

sections.title: 1.2 Missing waits, unusual waits, and bias
sections.html:
A missing value is a measurement not available for a known case: visit 109 exists, but its wait is unknown. An outlier is an unusually distant observed value: 31 minutes deserves checking, but distance does not prove error. Bias is systematic distortion; for example, if long waits are less likely to be entered, the observed service percentage will look too favorable. Exploratory analysis uses anomalies to ask questions before imposing conclusions (National Institute of Standards and Technology [NIST], n.d.).

Worked audit. There are 9 distinct visits, 8 numeric waits, and 1 missing wait. Thus wait completeness is 8/9=88.9%8/9=88.9\%, and missingness is 1/9=11.1%1/9=11.1\%: the 5% guardrail fails. Preserve the 31-minute value pending a timestamp check. Flag it for review; do not replace it with 10, zero, or a blank. Filtering only to complete waits changes the denominator from nine visits to eight measured visits, so label which denominator every result uses.

Excel check. With genuinely empty missing cells in the reconciled Table, =COUNT(Visits[WaitMin]) returns 8, =COUNTBLANK(Visits[WaitMin]) returns 1, and =COUNTA(Visits[VisitID]) returns 9. Also inspect text entries such as "N/A": a blank-cell count alone will not identify every missing-value code. Microsoft documents that COUNTBLANK counts empty cells and even formulas returning empty text (Microsoft, n.d.-c).

SPSS check. Declare any imported text or numeric missing-value code appropriately; leave visit 109 as missing, not zero. A frequency or data inspection should agree on nine cases and eight valid waits. Chart Builder can exclude cases with missing chart variables, so check the displayed base rather than assuming every chart includes nine visits (IBM, n.d.-a).

Failure mode: Dropping the missing visit and then calling the remaining eight “all visits.”

Try it — ungraded. If the service log recovers a valid wait for visit 109, what is the new missingness percentage? Explained answer: 0/9 = 0%. The denominator remains nine distinct visits; only the completeness status changes. The KPI itself cannot be updated until the recovered number is known.

sections.title: 2. Describe categories and the KPI
2.1 Category counts and denominators
sections.html:
A categorical summary counts labels rather than averaging them. In this case, channel is a label: “Walk-in” and “Scheduled” are not numeric scores. Use a frequency table when exact category counts matter, and a bar chart when a quick comparison matters. Penn State presents frequency tables and bars as ways to describe categorical observations (Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b).

Worked summary. Count the nine distinct visits, including the visit with missing wait. Walk-in IDs are 101, 103, 105, 107, and 109: 5/9 = 55.6%. Scheduled IDs are 102, 104, 106, and 108: 4/9 = 44.4%. Check that 5+4=95+4=9 and that the percentages total approximately 100%, allowing for rounding. This describes the extract’s channel mix, not the mix of all future customers. For a bar display, use a zero count baseline, labels “visits,” and bars of heights 5 and 4.

Tool check. In Excel, =COUNTIF(Visits[Channel],"Walk-in") returns 5 and the analogous "Scheduled" formula returns 4. In SPSS, Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies can produce category counts; check their total against nine reconciled cases (IBM, n.d.-b).

Failure mode: Reporting 5/8 as the walk-in share because one walk-in has a missing wait. Channel is observed for that visit.

Try it — ungraded. What share of distinct visits arrived on Thursday? Explained answer: IDs 107 and 108 are Thursday visits, so 2/9 = 22.2%. Both belong in this denominator even though one has an unusual wait.

sections.title: 2.2 Compute the service KPI without hiding uncertainty
sections.html:
A KPI is a measure tied to a decision; this one counts visits served within 10 minutes. Specify the comparison sign: a wait of exactly 10 minutes counts as meeting “within 10.” Specify the base separately: a measured-visit KPI excludes unknown waits but must disclose how many were excluded.

Worked calculation. Among eight recorded waits, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 meet the rule; 31 does not. The observed complete-case KPI is 7/8=87.5%7/8=\mathbf{87.5\%}. It is below the provisional 90% target. Now bound the effect of the one unknown wait without inventing it. If visit 109 was late, the all-visit result would be 7/9=77.8%7/9=\mathbf{77.8\%}; if it met the rule, it would be 8/9=88.9%8/9=\mathbf{88.9\%}. Even that favorable bound is below 90%. These are scenario bounds for these nine visits, not confidence intervals for next week.

Tool check. Excel =COUNTIF(Visits[WaitMin],"<=10") returns 7; =COUNT(Visits[WaitMin]) returns 8. Divide the first by the second for 87.5%. Recheck the result by marking each of the eight numeric waits “meets” or “does not meet.” In SPSS, inspect the eight valid waits, code the <=10 rule only for observed numeric waits, and compare the resulting counts 7 and 1 with the hand tally. A missing wait must remain unknown rather than become a failure or a success by default.

Failure mode: Reporting “87.5% of customers” without the qualifier of visits with recorded waits.

Try it — ungraded. If the target were instead 85%, would the measured-visit KPI pass, and would the missingness guardrail pass? Explained answer: The measured KPI would pass because 87.5% exceeds 85%. The quality guardrail would still fail because 11.1% missing exceeds 5%. A target change cannot repair incomplete evidence.

sections.title: 3. Describe the wait distribution
3.1 Center, spread, and a sensitivity check
sections.html:
A distribution shows which numeric values occur and how they are spread. The mean is the sum divided by the number measured; the median is the middle value after sorting. Use both when a long wait may pull the mean upward. Spread describes variation, not a second kind of average. Penn State introduces these descriptive measures and five-number summaries for quantitative data (Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b).

Worked calculation, in minutes. Sort the eight observed waits: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 31.

  1. Sum: 4+5+6+7+8+9+10+31=804+5+6+7+8+9+10+31=80. Mean: 80/8=1080/8=\mathbf{10} minutes.
  2. The middle positions are fourth and fifth: median =(7+8)/2=7.5=(7+8)/2=\mathbf{7.5} minutes.
  3. Range: 31−4=2731-4=\mathbf{27} minutes. Seven waits lie between 4 and 10; the eighth is 31.
  4. For an explicit sample standard deviation, deviations from the mean of 10 have squared values 36,25,16,9,4,1,0,44136,25,16,9,4,1,0,441. They total 532. Divide by 8−1=78-1=7, then take the square root: 532/7=8.72\sqrt{532/7}=\mathbf{8.72} minutes, rounded. This spread measure is highly affected by 31.

For a sensitivity check, temporarily set 31 aside only to understand its influence. The remaining sum is 80−31=4980-31=49, so their mean is 49/7=749/7=\mathbf{7} minutes; their median is also 7. Report both versions and retain 31 in the primary summary while its source is checked. The drop from mean 10 to mean 7 shows why verification matters; it does not justify deletion.

Tool check. Excel =AVERAGE(Visits[WaitMin]), =MEDIAN(Visits[WaitMin]), and =STDEV.S(Visits[WaitMin]) should return 10, 7.5, and approximately 8.72. STDEV.S uses n−1n-1 for a sample; do not confuse it with STDEV.P (Microsoft, n.d.-d). In SPSS, place WaitMin in Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore and compare its valid count and descriptive output with the hand results (IBM, n.d.-c).

Failure mode: Calling 10 minutes “what a typical customer waited” without showing the median and the 31-minute observation.

Try it — ungraded. If the verified 31-minute wait was actually 11 minutes, what would the eight-wait mean be? Explained answer: Replace 31 with 11: new sum 80−31+11=6080-31+11=60, then 60/8=7.560/8=\mathbf{7.5} minutes. This hypothetical does not amend the source record.

sections.title: 3.2 Quartiles, outlier flags, and honest bins
sections.html:
Quartiles divide sorted values into portions; the interquartile range (IQR) is the third quartile minus the first. A common exploratory flag is a value above Q3+1.5×IQRQ_3+1.5\times IQR. Methods for computing quartiles can differ across software, so state the convention and check plotted results rather than assuming identical boxplots. An outlier flag is a request to inspect a value, not a rule to erase it (NIST, n.d.; IBM, n.d.-d).

Worked check using the median-of-halves convention. The lower half is 4, 5, 6, 7, giving Q1=(5+6)/2=5.5Q_1=(5+6)/2=\mathbf{5.5}. The upper half is 8, 9, 10, 31, giving Q3=(9+10)/2=9.5Q_3=(9+10)/2=\mathbf{9.5}. Thus IQR=9.5−5.5=4IQR=9.5-5.5=\mathbf{4} minutes. The upper flag is 9.5+1.5(4)=15.59.5+1.5(4)=\mathbf{15.5} minutes. 31 exceeds it. The five-number summary under this convention is 4, 5.5, 7.5, 9.5, 31 minutes; a boxplot may show 31 as a separate point and end its upper whisker at 10.

For a small histogram, choose nonoverlapping minute bins and disclose their boundaries. With [0, 10), [10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40), the counts are 6, 1, 0, 1. The 10-minute wait belongs to the second bin. These bins explain shape; they do not directly count the KPI rule <=10. Do not read “six within 10” off this histogram.

Tool check. In Excel, sort the eight observed waits and reproduce the halves above; chart bins must match the stated boundaries. In SPSS Chart Builder, a scale WaitMin supports a histogram or a one-variable boxplot. Inspect plotted boundaries, outlier labels, and valid nn; IBM documents the boxplot gallery and its outlier display (IBM, n.d.-d).

Failure mode: Treating software quartiles, whiskers, or bin endpoints as universal without reading their definitions.

Try it — ungraded. How many observed waits fall in [5, 10)? Explained answer: Five: 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9. Four is excluded; 10 is excluded by the right-open boundary.

sections.title: 4. Choose evidence displays that answer a question
4.1 Match chart form to variable and decision
sections.html:
Use simple text for one decisive value, a table for exact figures, and a graph when a pattern or comparison matters. In this case, a channel-count bar chart compares categories; a histogram or boxplot shows numeric waits. A day-by-day line would suggest a continuous trend, although Friday’s wait is missing and each of Monday–Thursday has only two measured visits. NIST treats graphics as a way to uncover structure and anomalies, not as a substitute for inspecting data (NIST, n.d.).

Worked display choice. To ask, “Are most measured waits short, with a possible long tail?”, use the section 3 histogram: bin counts 6, 1, 0, 1, labeled visits against wait (minutes). Add “8 recorded waits; 1 of 9 visits missing.” To ask, “Which channel contributed how many visits?”, use the section 2 two-bar chart: 5 walk-in, 4 scheduled, with a zero baseline. Neither chart says staffing caused waits.

A daily table is safer than a trend line here. Measured daily medians are Monday (4+5)/2=4.5(4+5)/2=\mathbf{4.5}, Tuesday (6+7)/2=6.5(6+7)/2=\mathbf{6.5}, Wednesday (8+9)/2=8.5(8+9)/2=\mathbf{8.5}, and Thursday (10+31)/2=20.5(10+31)/2=\mathbf{20.5} minutes, each with n = 2. Friday has n = 0 measured waits, not a zero-minute median. Display that absence. Error bars require a defined quantity and uncertainty method, which belongs with later sampling work; two-observation daily medians do not warrant a confident trend claim.

Tool route. In Excel, build charts from the reconciled summary counts and label the axes and base. In SPSS Chart Builder, choose a bar display for categorical counts, a histogram for scale waits, or a boxplot for their distribution; check the chosen variable’s measurement level and the valid case count (IBM, n.d.-d).

Failure mode: Connecting four daily points and predicting Friday, or showing an unlabeled error bar that viewers mistake for the data’s full range.

Try it — ungraded. Which is better for giving the manager the exact number of Friday visits and recorded Friday waits: a line or a two-column table? Explained answer: A table. It can say “visits: 1; recorded waits: 0” without implying a Friday wait of zero.

sections.title: 4.2 Edit for attention without editing the evidence
sections.html:
Visual hierarchy directs attention using position, size, and contrast. Clutter consumes attention without helping the question. For Cedar Lane’s KPI display, the evidence to foreground is “7 of 8 recorded waits met 10 minutes; 1 of 9 visits lacks a wait.” Put that statement above the chart, rather than highlighting only 87.5%. Use consistent units, readable labels, and a text description for readers who cannot use the image. W3C recommends text alternatives that convey the essential information in complex charts (World Wide Web Consortium [W3C], n.d.).

Worked edit. Start with a draft showing eight individual waits as colored 3-D bars, a legend repeating visit IDs, and no missing-data note. Replace it with a sorted, two-column table of visit ID and wait (minutes), plus a clearly labeled marker beside 31: “unverified; check source timestamp.” State “8 measured of 9 distinct visits.” The result keeps every observation while making the unusual one easy to inspect. If individual visit IDs should not be shared outside the team, replace the ID column in the managerial version with anonymous row labels; retain the restricted audit table separately. Aesthetics must not override privacy or accuracy.

Points suit individual observations; lines suit ordered sequences; bars suit category comparisons; area can suggest totals over a continuous axis and is unnecessary here. Avoid 3-D effects, decorative contrast, or a cropped bar-chart axis that exaggerates a difference. A scatterplot needs two quantitative variables measured on the same visits: this extract has only one such variable, wait. Do not manufacture an x-variable to make a relationship graph.

Failure mode: Removing the 31-minute point because the revised chart looks cleaner.

Try it — ungraded. A slide shows “87.5% met target” in large type and hides “1 wait missing” in a footnote. What single edit most improves honesty? Explained answer: Place “7/8 recorded waits; 1/9 visits missing” beside the percentage. Viewers can then identify both the numerator and the evidence gap.

sections.title: 5. Validate and communicate a bounded decision
5.1 Independent checks and a reproducible record
sections.html:
A reproducible analysis preserves the input, the rule used to change it, and the outputs another analyst should obtain. Here, keep the untouched 10-row export; document that duplicate 104 was confirmed as a repeated export; save the nine-visit analysis table; and retain a short data dictionary defining WaitMin in minutes and a blank as unknown. Sorting or filtering for inspection must not quietly redefine the analysis population. Excel Tables make the included rows easier to see, but their formulas still need a denominator check (Microsoft, n.d.-a; Microsoft, n.d.-b).

Worked validation ledger. Before making a recommendation, independently confirm:

CheckExpected result
Raw export rows / distinct verified visits10 / 9
Numeric waits / missing waits8 / 1
Channel counts5 walk-in + 4 scheduled = 9
Sum of numeric waits80 minutes
Waits meeting <=10 / valid waits7 / 8
Mean / median10 / 7.5 minutes

Recount the waits by hand, then compare with Excel and SPSS. If a tool shows 9 valid waits, investigate whether blank 109 was converted to zero. If it shows 10 visits, revisit the duplicate. If an AI assistant suggests a formula or chart, test its output against this ledger and inspect its missing-value rule; fluent prose is not an independent check.

Failure mode: Sharing only a chart. Without the retained rows, inclusion rule, and definitions, a colleague cannot explain a changed KPI.

Try it — ungraded. A colleague obtains a mean of 80/9 = 8.89 minutes from the current table. What went wrong? Explained answer: The sum 80 covers eight measured waits, not nine measured waits. The known visit with missing wait belongs in a visit count, but it contributes no numeric value to the mean; 80/8=1080/8=10 minutes.

sections.title: 5.2 Separate observation, assumption, and recommendation
sections.html:
Descriptive observation reports these records. An inference extends beyond them and needs a defensible sampling basis. An assumption fills a gap openly. A recommendation states what to do given the evidence and limits. Keeping those sentences distinct prevents a short convenience extract from becoming a claim about next week’s demand. Penn State notes that representativeness matters when generalizing from observed cases to a population (Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a).

Worked manager note. Observation: “In the nine distinct visits recorded September 7–11, eight have waits. Seven of those eight met 10 minutes (87.5%), and one wait is missing (11.1% of visits). The recorded median is 7.5 minutes; one recorded wait is 31 minutes.” Assumption and limit: “The 31-minute value is provisionally retained until timestamp verification. These few convenience observations do not establish next week’s rate or the effect of staffing.” Recommendation: “Do not authorize an extended staffing schedule solely from this extract. Verify visits 108 and 109, repair wait capture, and collect a defined period covering busy and quiet desk hours. Reassess staffing against the service target and missingness guardrail with the fuller record.”

This recommendation does not say the desk is performing well. Even the favorable missing-wait scenario yields 8/9 = 88.9%, below the fictional 90% target for these visits. It says the proposed staffing change has not yet been evaluated with adequate evidence. Later sessions introduce sampling intervals, comparisons, and tests; a descriptive percentage alone does not establish a causal staffing benefit.

Failure mode: “The target was missed, so extending hours will fix it.” The first clause describes a small extract; the second asserts an untested intervention.

Try it — ungraded. Rewrite “Scheduled pickups cause long waits” as a supportable observation using this case. Explained answer: “The 31-minute recorded wait was for one scheduled pickup.” One observation identifies a case for investigation; it does not establish a channel effect or causality.

sections.title: Recap
sections.html:
• [KEY] Count cases at the declared grain before calculating a KPI. Ten export rows represented nine verified visits.
  • Report both a metric’s numerator and denominator: seven of eight recorded waits met 10 minutes.
  • Keep a known visit with a missing wait in visit counts; do not turn its wait into zero.
  • Inspect an unusual value against its source. A statistical flag does not prove a recording error.
  • Show center and spread together: mean 10, median 7.5, and one recorded wait of 31 minutes.
  • State bin boundaries and quartile conventions so another analyst can reproduce a chart.
  • Choose a table for exact small counts, bars for categories, and a histogram or boxplot for numeric shape.
  • [KEY] Separate what these records show from what might happen next week. This extract cannot establish a staffing effect.
  • Preserve the raw file, reconciliation decision, definitions, formulas, and independent check totals.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
• Bias: A systematic distortion, such as long waits being recorded less often.
  • Categorical variable: A label such as pickup channel, summarized with counts.
  • Convenience extract: Available records not selected to represent the intended population.
  • Denominator: The cases a fraction is based on; the observed KPI uses eight recorded waits.
  • Distribution: The pattern of values, including their center, spread, and unusual observations.
  • Grain: What one data row represents; here, one pickup visit.
  • Interquartile range (IQR): Third quartile minus first quartile, describing the middle portion’s spread.
  • KPI: A measure tied to a decision, such as the share meeting a wait-time rule.
  • Mean: Sum of numeric values divided by their numeric count.
  • Median: Middle value, or average of the two middle values, after sorting.
  • Missing value: An unavailable measurement for a case known to exist.
  • Outlier: An unusually distant observed value that merits investigation.
  • Population: The full set of cases relevant to a question; here, next week’s desk visits.
  • Provenance: Where records and values originated and how they were handled.
  • Sensitivity check: Recalculating under a stated alternative to see what changes.
